C005.subject: Rapid short-term GDP growth in low-income countries
C005.object: improvements in basic health and education metrics when growth is driven primarily by natural resource extraction
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Rapid short-term GDP growth in low-income countries improvements in basic health and education metrics when growth is driven primarily by natural resource extraction]

[PATH:empirical] Country-level panel data analysis comparing health/education outcomes (e.g., infant mortality, primary school enrollment) across low-income countries with natural resource booms (e.g., oil, minerals) versus those with non-resource growth, controlling for initial conditions and governance. — Direct test of the hypothesis using longitudinal data; can isolate the effect of resource-driven growth on human capital metrics over short-term horizons.

[PATH:empirical] Case studies of specific low-income countries that experienced rapid resource-driven growth (e.g., Angola, Papua New Guinea) with before-and-after comparisons of health and education indicators, including qualitative analysis of policy responses and resource allocation. — Provides contextual depth and causal mechanisms; can reveal whether negative correlations are due to neglect of social sectors, institutional failures, or other factors.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical models of the 'resource curse' applied to human capital investment, such as extensions of the Dutch disease model or political economy frameworks linking resource revenues to reduced government accountability for public services. — Explains potential causal pathways from resource-driven growth to underinvestment in health/education, helping to interpret empirical findings and identify confounders.

scope.domain: low-income countries, short-term (1–5 years), resource-driven growth

C006.subject: Rapid short-term GDP growth in low-income countries
C006.object: improvements in basic health and education metrics
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Rapid short-term GDP growth in low-income countries improvements in basic health and education metrics]

[PATH:empirical] World Bank Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS) paired with national accounts data from the IMF World Economic Outlook — Analyzing short-term (1–5 year) changes in GDP per capita against contemporaneous changes in child mortality, immunization rates, and primary school enrollment across low-income countries can directly test whether rapid growth coincides with health/education improvements.

[PATH:literature] Journal of Development Economics: systematic review or meta-analysis of studies on growth-poverty-health linkages in low-income settings — A meta-analysis can aggregate findings from multiple country-case studies and panel regressions to determine the empirical consensus on whether short-term GDP spurts lead to measurable gains in basic human capital metrics.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical model: health-led growth vs. growth-led health frameworks (e.g., Bloom, Canning, and Sevilla 2004) — Examining theoretical models that posit bidirectional causality can clarify mechanisms—if health improvements drive growth rather than vice versa, short-term GDP spikes may not reliably produce health/education gains without pre-existing institutional or public health capacity.

C007.subject: Sustained GDP growth in high-income countries
C007.object: increases in social trust on subjective life satisfaction
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Sustained GDP growth in high-income countries increases in social trust on subjective life satisfaction]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal panel data from the World Values Survey and European Social Survey, comparing within-country changes in GDP per capita, social trust, and life satisfaction over 10+ years in high-income nations. — Directly tests the moderation hypothesis by examining whether the slope of social trust on life satisfaction declines as GDP grows, controlling for individual and country-level confounders.

[PATH:empirical] Experimental or quasi-experimental studies on the effect of economic growth on value priorities (e.g., Inglehart's post-materialism thesis), using repeated cross-sectional data to assess whether materialist values crowd out relational well-being sources. — Provides evidence for the proposed mechanism that GDP growth shifts priorities away from non-material factors like trust, thereby weakening their impact on life satisfaction.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing studies on the relationship between social trust and subjective well-being, stratified by national income level and growth rate, to identify systematic differences in effect sizes. — Synthesizes available evidence to determine if the negative moderation pattern is robust across high-income contexts and sustained growth periods, addressing the disputed status.

qualifier.mechanism: GDP growth crowds out non-material sources of well-being, weakening their contribution to life satisfaction

C008.subject: Sustained GDP growth in high-income countries
C008.object: improvements in subjective life satisfaction across all income levels
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Sustained GDP growth in high-income countries improvements in subjective life satisfaction across all income levels]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal panel data from the World Values Survey (WVS) and Gallup World Poll, focusing on OECD countries from 1990-2020, stratified by income quintile. — Directly tests the correlation between per capita GDP growth and self-reported life satisfaction across income levels, controlling for country and year fixed effects.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of published studies on the Easterlin Paradox, specifically examining high-income countries with sustained growth periods >10 years. — Synthesizes existing findings to determine whether the hypothesized positive correlation holds consistently or is refuted by the well-documented satiation effects in wealthy nations.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical model incorporating relative income and adaptation effects (e.g., Kahneman & Krueger's set-point theory) applied to OECD data. — Provides a causal framework to explain why GDP growth may not translate to improved life satisfaction for all income levels, offering a testable counter-hypothesis.

[PATH:empirical] Comparative panel data analysis of GDP growth, volatility, and inequality indices (e.g., World Bank WDI, UNU-WIDER) against subjective wellbeing metrics (e.g., Gallup World Poll, OECD Better Life Index) over 5-15 year horizons across all countries. — Directly tests the hypothesis by controlling for volatility and inequality, assessing whether growth consistently correlates with wellbeing improvements in the medium term.

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal case studies of countries with high GDP volatility or high inequality (e.g., commodity-dependent economies, rapidly industrializing nations) tracking changes in health, education, and life satisfaction over 5-15 years. — Provides granular evidence on whether growth benefits persist under adverse conditions, refuting or supporting the 'irrespective' claim.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical models of welfare economics (e.g., Sen's capabilities approach, Easterlin paradox literature) that formalize the relationship between aggregate growth and individual wellbeing under risk and distributional constraints. — Clarifies mechanisms and boundary conditions, helping to interpret empirical findings and assess the plausibility of direct enhancement without moderating factors.
